Meatless Meat

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
What makes a nugget a nugget, and can a burger be veggie?

Unique Selling Point:
Plant-based protein meat alternatives is gaining traction on the South African market. People are starting to realise the benefits of eating less meat, opting for meat analogues... i.e. products that take the shape and flavour of meat, but is made from meatless proteins. But the Department of Agriculture is stepping on the industry's toes, claiming that they have no right labelling something as a sausage, or patty if it contains no actual meat. Why? it causes confusion amongst customers, they say... and meatless meat is not covered by comprehensive legislation, unlike traditional meat. So they have ordered the Food Safety Association of SA to seize "wrongly labelled" vegetarian and vegan products from the shelves of retailers. but the Meatless meat industry is not taking this lying down...

Summary:
In 2018, Natalia Fernandez and her husband started a small company from their kitchen in Johannesburg. They had been experimenting with using various beans as an alternative to meat in creating a range of different burger patties. Through tireless marketing and hard work, they now stock Meraki Burgers in major retailers across the country. And people are loving the flavours. But, they are facing a crisis. According to the Department of Agriculture thay cannot call their products patties, or burgers... since it doesn't contain any meat. Retailers have scaled down orders, because they are scared of the products being seized by the FSA. And the cost of re-branding and relabelling their products is huge. So what now?

On the 19th of August the Consumer Goods Council of SA, backed by various pro-plant based organisations, manufacturers and distributors won an interdict against the Department, temporarily halting the seizure of meatless meat. But the fight is far from over.

Further information:
In the National Climate Change Response White Paper, the South African government admits that “land-based human activities, such as forest clearing and unsustainable agricultural practices, are not only increasing Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions from these sources, but are also reducing the earth’s natural ability to absorb GHGs”. The White Paper also states that “[t]he evidence that current global warming is due to human activities associated with industrialisation and modern agriculture is overwhelming”.
Yet, now, this very government’s Department of Agriculture, Land Reform and Rural Development is aiming to disrupt a prosperous economic sector that could help South Africans mitigate their carbon footprint.
What the White Paper fails to mention is that the farming and eating of animals is a leading contributor to the global climate crisis, responsible for about 20% of GHG emissions, and that switching to a plant-based diet could reduce an individual’s food-related emissions by up to 50%.

But it is not just plant-based meat alternatives that have come under fire. Following a supposed meeting between DALRRD and the Food Safety Agency, another letter was sent, this time to Woolworths, one of the largest supermarket chains in the country. The supermarket giant was instructed that the plant-based egg substitute Just Egg could not be sold as “eggs” as it does not hail from domestic fowl.

ProVeg Director, Donovan Will says there is no evidence that consumers are confused. No-one is accidentally buying a bean-protein sausage and harmed when eating it... in fact, it would seem that the only industry benefitting from this move would be meat producers in South Africa.

Script:


MEATLESS MEAT




It’s Saturday afternoon… The fire is just right, and the beers are cold…. The guests are on their way

But imagine the horror when you discover that your boerewors… is not actually … well… wors… … and the burgers, are beans!





Doorbell…

PANIC
Link 1
Fridge
Burger Patty
As silly as it may seem, this is what some believe happens on a regular basis… Confused consumers duped into buying meat products that contain no meat…
V/O
Shots of the letter



In fact, the Department of Agriculture, Land Reform and Rural Development is so serious about this, that it has drawn a line in the sand… outlawing the use of “meaty” names for non-meat products…
Link 2 Cont
Patty in pan
Apparently, words like biltong, sausage, nugget and even burger belong exclusively to meat… and the Department has a beef with these… so-called meat analogues…
Billy Makhafola
00:00:04:05 - 00:00:25:11
Meat analogues? The definition, if you want to put it clearly, is just, it's just fake meat. They, they normally call them plant-based…
V/O
Billy Makhafola is the Executive Officer of the Agricultural Standards Act at the Department of Agriculture, Land Reform and Rural Development. He’s in charge of regulating the classification, packing and labeling of processed meat products for sale in South Africa.
Billy Makhafola
The fact of the matter is we have realised over some time that product names, that are regulated, that are exclusively reserved for meat products are actually used in the sale of meat analogs.
V/O
It’s a sentiment echoed by many of our meat producers, who believe in the exclusive use of “meaty names”.
Peter Gordon
We would like simply that the products that are plant based carry names that are not misleading and that accurately reflect the ingredients that are used in the products.


V/O
Peter Gordon is a meat man – CEO of the South African Meat Processors’ Association, or SAMPA.
Peter Gordon
Derek: What names shouldn't be used?
00:01:57:15 - 00:02:28:04
Well, certainly we believe they are names like bratwurst, biltong. Those names we believe belong exclusively. Schnitzel would be another example. And clearly, when you use the name meat or chicken or beef in a descriptor, it should be a product that actually contains that ingredient.


V/O
In South Africa meat analogs have been around since the early 90s, and the industry has enjoyed significant growth, especially over the last few years. Today, many people choose plant-based meat alternatives for a variety of reasons…
Donovan Will
I ate meat for 30 years and when I stopped eating meat, it wasn't because of the taste. It wasn't because I didn't enjoy a good burger at the braai. It was for environmental reasons,
for ethical reasons, health reasons.


V/O
Donovan Will is the CEO of ProVeg South Africa… He’s a vegan who enjoys a “meaty” burger from time to time…. As long as it’s plant-based…
Donovan Will
Why shouldn't we be allowed to have something that if it looks like a chicken burger tastes like a chicken burger, you know, it does everything that a chicken burger does. Why can't we call it a vegetarian chicken style burger? No one's trying to pretend that it's actually chicken…
V/O

Product jump cut
But apparently the mere use of the word “chicken” or “beef” on the packaging, may mislead consumers…
Peter Gordon
00:03:53:15 - 00:04:16:27
I think they certainly are some products where people could pick up a pack, think they're buying a beef sausage or a lamb sausage and actually get home and find they haven't got what they wanted. And that's what we are trying to prevent.
V/O
But this is not just about customer confusion… it's also about regulation…
Billy Makhafola
00:01:38:20 - 00:01:56:09
The problem kicks in when you have a standard that is associated with this product name and that standard is not applied when that name is invoked


elsewhere in the sale of that very product.
V/O

Visuals, Derek with Documents
But instead of accommodating both the meat and plant-based varieties of a particular product… The Agricultural Products Standards Act of 1990 and its various amendments… set out specifically what processed meat should and shouldn’t contain… For example, the meat to fat ratio, and specific ingredients which may or may not be used.
LINK 3


So the problem is, when you produce a plant-based sausage, for example… it contains no meat, no animal fat… almost none of the ingredients used in traditional meat processing… so technically it does not comply with the law…
V/O
And if – according to the law – this sausage is not actually a sausage… you cannot label it as such. You can’t even call it a “veggie sausage”...
Billy Makhafola
00:08:20:11 - 00:09:01:22
If you look at Section six of the act, it actually prohibit misleading labels or claims. Even if you use a product name in conjunction with another name or other words, that is still prohibited.
V/O
In June this year, the Department dropped a bombshell. In order to comply with the law.. all meat analogs and meat replacement products need to be renamed and relabeled… with immediate effect.
Natalia Kostanova Fernandez
00:03:02:29 - 00:03:34:15
It's been a terrible few months, to be honest, in terms of our orders. You know, they definitely plummeted because retailers were not sure about what the next steps were going to be.


V/O
Natalia Kostanova Fernandez, owner of Meraki Plant Based Food, has been producing a range of vegan burger patties since 2018.
Natalia Kostanova Fernandez
0:01:13:28 - 00:01:36:03
When we first began, people were a little bit hesitant to stock our products. I think primarily because we are bean based and we're not an analogue meat as such.
V/O
Despite the fact that her bean burger patties do not try to imitate meat in any way, she’s also been caught in the crossfire. Companies like Meraki were given just two months to comply with the Department’s new labeling regulations. And non-compliance would have severe consequences…
Natalia Kostanova Fernandez
I think about on the 18th of August, we were told that our products would be seized on the 22nd of August. So obviously, you know, it's millions and millions of rands worth of products. We didn't really know what was going to happen with the product when it was seized, if it was going to be stored in the correct conditions.
V/O
Then, just days before the Food Safety Agency was due to start confiscating meat analogs, the Consumer Goods Council came to the rescue, obtaining a last-minute court interdict against the Department’s plans. Despite buying them time until the 17th of November, the plant-based industry is facing a real challenge.
Natalia Kostanova Fernandez
00:04:20:03 - 00:04:24:25
Derek: Is this a move that could cost your company a considerable amount of money?

00:04:25:06 - 00:04:50:27
Absolutely. Yes. You know, should it go forward and we have to remove all of the products from the shelves and it will be a considerable financial loss for us. Especially for us being a very small company, we do everything financially ourselves. So it could essentially, you know, make us close our doors, which is it would be devastating.
Donovan Will
We are currently in a situation where a lot of the product's prices are coming down. You know, we are trying to get to parity and unfortunately having to change labels, having to hire lawyers to find out what's happening. Having to delay the import of products because we're not sure if they're going to be seized.

00:21:49:18 - 00:22:06:17
These things all costs money. And when a company incurs these costs, obviously, unfortunately, these costs are going to be handed over to the consumer.


V/O
At a time of significant global pressure for us to cut meat consumption to reduce our carbon footprint, many have questioned the Department’s timing and motives…
Billy Makhafola
00:15:37:22 - 00:15:42:22
Are you trying to push meat sales?
No. No, we shouldn't. Remember, we are not against meat analogs at all. Our concern is to regulate whatever gets sold, to protect the consumer at the same time, so there’s a level playing field in terms of product that is actually being put out for sale between all the traders.


Peter Gordon
00:08:36:09 - 00:08:44:04
Do you acknowledge that there's a real need to change our eating habits? Consumption of meat.

00:08:45:02 - 00:09:14:03
I think there's a need for people to have the freedom to choose to eat what they want to eat. And I think people have the right to decide whether they want to eat a vegetarian product, a vegan product, a plant based product, or a combination or a meat product.
LINK
Delicious… but the proposed changes to meat analogue labeling presents a challenge… What do we call this, if we’re no longer allowed to call it a burger?
Natalia Kostanova Fernandez
00:06:25:20 - 00:06:49:13
We were using the word patty, but that's not allowed. So, yes, thinking out of the box, possibly a fritter, a disk. I mean, that sounds really unappealing. I think we may call it a bean based thingamajig.
V/O
And while the meat analogue sector gets its head around its patties, disks, and thingamajigs, the Department of Agriculture is adamant that if it’s not made from animal flesh… it’s simply not a burger…
Billy Makhafola
00:11:13:03 - 00:11:22:02
Derek: I have to be honest, in some respects this seems rather petty…
00:11:23:11 - 00:11:58:23
Well. Well, the law is the law. It has to be implemented. The minute you actually evoke those names that are associated with processed meat product, you are actually inviting us. Otherwise we don't have any problem with meat analogs.
Donovan Will
00:15:26:07 - 00:15:33:28
Would you say there are more serious challenges facing our country than the labelling of meat substitutes?

00:15:34:15 - 00:16:05:03
So I think everyone knows that South Africa has a lot of issues that the government really should be prioritizing instead of worrying about people, whether or not people are confused about a veggie burger.

00:16:21:18 - 00:16:34:03
But you're not looking at the worst case scenario. Somebody walks into a supermarket and walks away with what they think is a real meat burger, and it's a veggie burger.

00:16:34:26 - 00:16:40:17
And the worst thing would be if they actually got home and. Enjoyed it and had to tell all their friends that they actually enjoyed the veggie burger.









PROMO 1 11”
The Plant-based meat industry is under threat as the government demands the relabelling of all these products. But, what do you call this if we’re no longer allowed to call it a burger?
PROMO 2 21”
Should some words like nugget, sausage and even burger be reserved exclusively for processed meat products?
UPSOUND: Donovan Will
if it looks like a chicken burger tastes like a chicken burger, does everything that a chicken burger does. Why can't we call it a vegetarian chicken-style burger? No one's trying to pretend that it's actually chicken…
We take a bite into the big Veggie burger debate!


PROMO 3 21”
Derek: This innocent-looking burger is at the centre of a nation-wide dispute because it’s made of plants…

UPSOUND: Donovan Will
Well, the law is the law. It has to be implemented..
What is the Department of Agriculture’s beef with plant-based meat?

UPSOUND: Billy Makhafola
Well, the law is the law. It has to be implemented..

metadata.Unique Selling Point: Plant-based protein meat alternatives is gaining traction on the South African market. People are starting to realise the benefits of eating less meat, opting for meat analogues... i.e. products that take the shape and flavour of meat, but is made from meatless proteins. But the Department of Agriculture is stepping on the industry's toes, claiming that they have no right labelling something as a sausage, or patty if it contains no actual meat. Why? it causes confusion amongst customers, they say... and meatless meat is not covered by comprehensive legislation, unlike traditional meat. So they have ordered the Food Safety Association of SA to seize "wrongly labelled" vegetarian and vegan products from the shelves of retailers. but the Meatless meat industry is not taking this lying down...
metadata.Summary: In 2018, Natalia Fernandez and her husband started a small company from their kitchen in Johannesburg. They had been experimenting with using various beans as an alternative to meat in creating a range of different burger patties. Through tireless marketing and hard work, they now stock Meraki Burgers in major retailers across the country. And people are loving the flavours. But, they are facing a crisis. According to the Department of Agriculture thay cannot call their products patties, or burgers... since it doesn't contain any meat. Retailers have scaled down orders, because they are scared of the products being seized by the FSA. And the cost of re-branding and relabelling their products is huge. So what now? On the 19th of August the Consumer Goods Council of SA, backed by various pro-plant based organisations, manufacturers and distributors won an interdict against the Department, temporarily halting the seizure of meatless meat. But the fight is far from over.
metadata.Further information: In the National Climate Change Response White Paper, the South African government admits that “land-based human activities, such as forest clearing and unsustainable agricultural practices, are not only increasing Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions from these sources, but are also reducing the earth’s natural ability to absorb GHGs”. The White Paper also states that “[t]he evidence that current global warming is due to human activities associated with industrialisation and modern agriculture is overwhelming”. Yet, now, this very government’s Department of Agriculture, Land Reform and Rural Development is aiming to disrupt a prosperous economic sector that could help South Africans mitigate their carbon footprint. What the White Paper fails to mention is that the farming and eating of animals is a leading contributor to the global climate crisis, responsible for about 20% of GHG emissions, and that switching to a plant-based diet could reduce an individual’s food-related emissions by up to 50%. But it is not just plant-based meat alternatives that have come under fire. Following a supposed meeting between DALRRD and the Food Safety Agency, another letter was sent, this time to Woolworths, one of the largest supermarket chains in the country. The supermarket giant was instructed that the plant-based egg substitute Just Egg could not be sold as “eggs” as it does not hail from domestic fowl. ProVeg Director, Donovan Will says there is no evidence that consumers are confused. No-one is accidentally buying a bean-protein sausage and harmed when eating it... in fact, it would seem that the only industry benefitting from this move would be meat producers in South Africa.
